title: Syllabus
text:
“Us and them” is one of the oldest structures in politics and one of the hardest to pin down. This seminar asks what happens to a democracy when that line hardens, and what group identity has to do with it.
We start with identity, where the concept comes from and how an attachment to a group becomes a political fact. Then we take the word “polarization” apart, because it names several different things and many arguments in this literature are really arguments about which one is meant. The middle of the term belongs to affective polarization, the tendency to dislike the other side rather than merely to disagree with it, and to the survey items that much of the evidence for it rests on. We end by pushing on the concept: what happens when the dividing line is religion or region rather than party, whether partisan animosity is about identity at all, and how much of the alleged damage to democracy holds up.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course objectives
The seminar is built around reading political science carefully rather than accumulating results. By the end of it you should be able to take a claim about polarization, work out what it is a claim about, and say what evidence would support or undermine it.
Three things run through every session. The first is conceptual discipline: polarization means several different things, and many disagreements in this literature are about which one is meant. The second is measurement: an affective polarization score is a construction, and what it is built from shapes what it can support. The third is evidence: a striking finding is a starting point rather than a conclusion, and the seminar asks what design produced it and how much it can carry.
The term paper is where you do this on a question of your own, with evidence you analyse yourself.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course logistics

General information
The seminar meets on Wednesdays, 15:30-17:00, in A5, 6 – C 112. Each session is built around the core reading, so the discussion only works if everyone has done it. Readings for each session are listed in Section 5 and the full references are collected in Section 6.






Tip



If you have to miss a session, tell me beforehand. A short email is enough, and it lets me tell you what you missed.




Prerequisites
Two different things go by this name, and it is worth keeping them apart.
Formally, the prerequisite depends on which of the two modules in Section 3.3 you register this seminar under. Whether you meet it is a question for the module catalogue and the Studienbüro, not for me.
In terms of what this course assumes, no prior work on polarization, party systems or political psychology is expected. The readings are research articles rather than textbook chapters, so you should be comfortable reading one, but learning how to read one is part of what the seminar is for.


Module and credits
This seminar is offered in both International Relations modules, and which one applies to you depends on how you register it. The credits, the assessment and the term paper word limit are the same either way. It counts toward either of:

Aufbaumodul: Internationale Beziehungen (Modulkatalog p. 31)
Schwerpunktmodul: Internationale Beziehungen (Modulkatalog p. 38)
Course type: Hauptseminar (HS)
Credits: 6 ECTS

The authoritative version of all of this is the module catalogue and the examination regulations for the B.A. Political Science, not this page. Where the two disagree, the regulations win.


What is required of you
Assessment has two parts, and the vocabulary is the examination regulations’ own. Coursework (Studienleistung) is assessed pass or fail, and passing it is a prerequisite for the graded work. The term paper (Prüfungsleistung) carries the mark.

Coursework, pass or fail
1. Active participation (Mitarbeit). Section 13b of the examination regulations allows participation to be set as coursework in a discussion-based course of this size, and it is set here. It is assessed on the whole of your contributions across the term, not on any single session. What counts is that you engage with the reading and with what other people say about it.
2. Doing the reading. Each session lists core reading, which everyone does, and optional reading, which is there for anyone who wants to go further and as a starting point for term papers. The core reading is mandatory rather than recommended. It is also the basis on which participation is assessed, because a discussion of a text nobody has read is not a discussion.
3. A term paper idea presentation (Referat). You pitch your term paper to the group in session 11 or 12. A few minutes on your question, why it is worth answering, and how you would answer it, followed by discussion. The point is to get criticism while there is still time to act on it.


Term paper, graded

Form: an empirical written term paper (schriftliche Hausarbeit), plus the code that reproduces its analysis.
Length: at most 7000 words, the limit set in the module catalogue.
Deadline: 15 January, 23:59.
Topic: your own, on something the seminar covers. You pitch it in session 11 or 12, and session 13 is optional individual consultation.

A workable paper takes a claim from the literature and confronts it with evidence you analyse yourself: it tests the claim against a case or a dataset it was not built on, re-analyses published data under a different measurement choice, or works out what two authors’ rival definitions do to the same data. A summary of what several authors have said is not a term paper, and neither is an argument that never meets data.






Important



Every paper produces results, and somebody else has to be able to recompute them. Hand in the script or the notebook that produced your numbers, tables and figures, together with the data or a link to where it comes from. Any technology is fine, R, Python, Stata or anything else, as long as the result comes out of a script that can be run again rather than out of clicks nobody can retrace.





Registration and withdrawal
Registration for the Prüfungsleistung, deregistration, and the applicable deadlines are handled by the Studienbüro under the examination regulations, not by me. Check the dates there and keep to them, because responsibility for meeting them sits with you.
If a good reason, illness in particular, prevents you from submitting the term paper on time, section 30 of the examination regulations applies. You must submit a written application to the Studienbüro without delay, with evidence. The examination board decides, and the burden of proof is on the applicant. Tell me as well, but telling me is not a substitute for the formal application.
Section 5 additionally allows deadlines for coursework and examinations to be extended on a timely written application, for instance for students with children or with dependants requiring care.


Disability and chronic illness
If a disability or a chronic illness makes it harder for you to take an assessment in the form it is set, you are entitled to compensation that restores equal opportunity, under section 6 of the examination regulations. Applications are made in writing and in good time, and applications on grounds of disability or chronic illness go to the university’s representative for students with disabilities or chronic illness.






Tip



Talk to me early, and tell me only what you want to. The formal route runs through the representative and the examination board, and I do not need to know the nature of your condition. What helps me is knowing early that an adjustment is coming, so it can be built in rather than improvised.




Language
The seminar is taught in English and the readings are in English. The term paper shall be written in English.


Additional learning resources
Two external platforms are worth your time. Both are voluntary and neither is part of the requirements to pass. They are here because the term paper asks for reproducible code, and this seminar spends its sessions on the reading rather than on tooling.
DataCamp. Use the link to join the course group, which gives you six months of premium access. DataCamp offers in-depth, self-paced practical training in R, coding, data analytics and AI topics, so it is the right place to drill something until it is automatic, at whatever speed suits you. The introduction to R track is a good starting point.






Warning



Register with your uni-mannheim.de address. Premium access is tied to the university account. If you sign up with a private address the group link will not grant it, and the fix is to start again with the right address.


Duolingo Math. Freemium, and a good starting point if you would like to relaunch yourself into mathematics fundamentals or introductory statistics. No prior statistics is assumed in this seminar, so this is not a prerequisite. It is simply there if the maths behind a reading feels shakier than you would like.


Mental health support
Life and study at the University of Mannheim can sometimes feel complicated, challenging, or overwhelming. That is completely normal.
If you ever feel mentally or emotionally strained, you may find useful advice on the university’s good mental health and studying page. The help in times of crisis page gives an overview of the counselling and support services available at the university.

title: Syllabus
text:
AI policy






Note



This stated policy is a first proposal and may be subject to change during the term.


You may use AI assistance, and for some things it is genuinely useful: finding literature, checking whether an argument holds together, working on your English.
Two conditions.
Declare it. Your term paper carries a short note saying what you used and what you used it for. A sentence is enough. An undeclared use is a problem in a way that a declared one is not.
It does not make the argument. The claim, the reasoning and the judgement about what the evidence supports have to be yours, because they are what is being assessed. A paper that reads as though nobody decided anything is a weak paper whether or not a model wrote it, and you are answerable for every sentence you submit, including any citation that turns out not to exist.

title: Syllabus
text:
Session plan
What each session covers, what you should be able to do afterwards, and what to read. Dates are on the Schedule.






Note



This is a preliminary plan and may be revised during the term.



Session 1: Introduction and outlook

09 September 2026

What the seminar asks, how the term is organised, and what a term paper in it looks like. We also settle the schedule for the term paper pitches.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Describe what the seminar covers and how the three substantive blocks build on one another.
State what the term paper asks for, when the pitch happens, and what makes a question workable.


Optional

Torcal and Harteveld (2025)




Session 2: What is identity?

16 September 2026 · Concepts

Before we can ask what divides a democracy, we need a concept of the groups that do the dividing. This session treats identity as a demand for recognition and dignity, and asks how an attachment to a group becomes a political fact rather than a private one.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Trace where the modern concept of identity comes from and how it entered political argument.
Explain how a demand for recognition becomes a political demand.
Distinguish an identity from a preference, and say why the distinction matters for the rest of the term.


Core reading

Fukuyama (2018), chapters 1, 2 and 3

Optional

Huddy (2013)
Huddy (2001)
Westphal (2025)




Session 3: What is political polarization?

23 September 2026 · Concepts







Note



The core reading for this session was listed incorrectly at first. The intended readings are the 2008 exchange in the Journal of Politics between Abramowitz and Saunders (2008) and Fiorina et al. (2008). The Annual Review article by Fiorina and Abrams (2008), listed here before, is now optional. If you have already read it, your time was not wasted: it makes the same case as the reply, at greater length and with the concepts spelled out.


Polarization is a metaphor borrowed from the natural sciences, and political science has attached it to several different things: how far apart elites stand, how far apart voters stand, how tightly issue positions bundle together, and how far apart the camps feel. This session sorts them apart and asks which disputes in the literature are empirical and which are definitional.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Distinguish elite from mass polarization, and ideological divergence from issue alignment.
Explain why two authors can disagree about whether a public is polarized without disagreeing about any fact.
Identify which concept of polarization a given empirical claim depends on.


Core reading

Abramowitz and Saunders (2008)
Fiorina et al. (2008)

Optional

Fiorina and Abrams (2008)
Lelkes (2016)
Baldassarri and Gelman (2008)
McCoy and Somer (2018)
Turkenburg and Erkel (2025)




Session 4: What is affective polarization?

30 September 2026 · Concepts

Affective polarization (AP) is the tendency of people who identify with a party to view opposing partisans negatively and copartisans positively (Iyengar and Westwood 2015; Iyengar et al. 2019). This session takes the concept apart: the social identity logic it rests on, what it claims to add to an ideological account of division, and what evidence shows that partisan animus reaches beyond survey answers into implicit attitudes and behavior.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Derive in-group favouritism and out-group hostility from social identity theory.
Explain what affective polarization claims to add to an ideological account of division.
Assess the evidence that partisan animus shows up in implicit attitudes and behavior, and not only in what people say in surveys.


Core reading

Iyengar et al. (2012)
Iyengar and Westwood (2015)

Optional

Wagner (2024)
Iyengar et al. (2019)
Tajfel and Turner (1986)
Reiljan (2020)
Iyengar and Wagner (2025)




Session 5: Measuring affective polarization

07 October 2026 · Measurement

Almost everything we know about AP rests on one class of survey item: feeling thermometers and like/dislike ratings. This session asks what that item captures, how single ratings are aggregated into one score when there are more than two parties, and how those construction choices move the estimates and the conclusions that rest on them.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Say what a feeling thermometer measures and what it does not.
Reconstruct how an AP score is built in a multiparty system, and state what each step of the construction assumes.
Explain why the decision about who counts as a partisan changes the population an estimate refers to.
Judge whether a published estimate supports a comparison across countries or over time.


Core reading

Druckman and Levendusky (2019)
Wagner (2021)

Optional

Gidron et al. (2022)
Tyler and Iyengar (2024)
Tichelbaecker et al. (2023)
Kekkonen and Ylä-Anttila (2021)
Torcal and Comellas (2025)
Carlin and Love (2025)




Session 6: Beyond the thermometer: behavioral measures

14 October 2026 · Measurement

An attitude scale asks people what they feel. A behavioral measure asks them to do something: to divide money, to extend trust, to choose between candidates. We work through conjoint allocation games fielded across EU member states, and ask what a behavioral measure buys and what it costs.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Describe how a conjoint allocation game turns a choice into a measure of partisan animosity.
Compare behavioral and attitudinal measures on what each can and cannot support.
Explain why coalition partnership changes the pattern of animosity in European party systems.


Core reading

Hahm et al. (2024)
Stoetzer et al. (2023)

Optional

Westwood et al. (2018)
Carlin and Love (2013)
Wagner and Praprotnik (2024)
Röllicke (2025)




Session 7: Beyond party: social sorting and non-partisan identities

21 October 2026 · Extensions and consequences

Party is not the only line people sort along. This session asks what happens when party, region, religion, ethnicity and referendum camps line up with one another, and what happens when they cut across instead.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Define social sorting and explain why an aligned cleavage structure raises out-group animus.
Give a case in which the polarizing identity is not partisan at all, and say what makes it behave like one.
Assess how much support the evidence gives the claim that cross-cutting identities dampen animus.


Core reading

Harteveld (2021)
Hobolt et al. (2020)

Optional

Hahm et al. (2023)
Bradley and Chauchard (2022)
Balcells and Kuo (2023)
Bettarelli et al. (2023)
Roccas and Brewer (2002)
Mason (2016)
Zollinger (2024)
Mason and Versteegen (2025)
Hobolt and Tilley (2025)




Session 8: Is partisanship a social identity, or a cue about ideology?

04 November 2026 · Extensions and consequences

American work is split on what partisan animosity is actually about. One side reads it as group identity, dislike of them because they are them (party over policy). The other reads a party label as shorthand for policy positions, so what looks like identity is disagreement in disguise (policy over party). We follow the exchange and ask what evidence could settle it.
Afterwards you will be able to:

State the party-over-policy and the policy-over-party positions and the evidence each rests on.
Explain why identity and categorisation are hard to separate in survey and experimental designs.
Specify what evidence would distinguish the two accounts, and why it is hard to obtain.


Core reading

Orr et al. (2023)
Dias and Lelkes (2022)

Optional

Orr and Huber (2020)
Dafoe et al. (2018)
Huddy et al. (2015)
Klar et al. (2018)
Bankert and Stone (2025)




Session 9: Consequences of affective polarization for democracy

11 November 2026 · Extensions and consequences

AP is usually introduced as a danger, to democratic norms, to accountability, to the willingness to live alongside people who vote differently. Recent work is more careful. Some of the alleged consequences do not survive better designs, and others hold only under particular conditions. This session separates what is established from what is asserted.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Reconstruct the argument for why AP is supposed to harm democracy.
Name the consequences that have actually been studied, and the designs used to study them.
Distinguish findings that hold up from findings that depend on context or on measurement.


Core reading

Harteveld et al. (2026)
Broockman et al. (2023)

Optional

Voelkel et al. (2023)
Versteegen et al. (2026)
Kekkonen and Harteveld (2025)
Somer and McCoy (2025)




Session 10: Open session

18 November 2026 · Extensions and consequences

This slot is deliberately unallocated. We settle the topic and the reading in the session before, so it can follow whatever the group most wants to pursue, whether that is a theme from earlier in the term or something none of the readings covered. Bring suggestions.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Propose a topic or a reading, and say what the seminar gains from it.
Read a text without a prepared framing, and take part in a discussion the group has shaped itself.



Session 11: Term paper pitches I

25 November 2026 · Term papers

Short pitches of your term paper plan, followed by discussion. Half the group presents and the other half asks the questions.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Present a research question, why it is worth answering, and a design that could answer it, in a few minutes.
Name the data or the texts your paper will work from.
Give another student criticism they can still act on.



Session 12: Term paper pitches II

02 December 2026 · Term papers

The second half of the pitches, in the same format.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Present a research question, why it is worth answering, and a design that could answer it, in a few minutes.
Name the data or the texts your paper will work from.
Give another student criticism they can still act on.



Session 13: Term paper consultation (optional)

09 December 2026 · Term papers

Optional individual consultation on the term paper. There is no group session in this slot. Email me to book a time.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Leave with a question, an outline and a plan you can execute before the deadline.

How a session runs
Everyone reads the core reading beforehand, and the session is a discussion of that text rather than a lecture about it. I open with a short framing of the reading and the questions it raises, and the rest of the time belongs to the group. The optional readings are there for anyone who wants to go further, and as a starting point for term papers.
Sessions 11 and 12 are term paper pitches, and session 13 is optional individual consultation. See what is required of you for what each of those asks.

title: Us and them: Identity and polarization in contemporary democracies
text: Fall 2026 Department of Political Science School of Social Sciences University of Mannheim

title: Us and them: Identity and polarization in contemporary democracies
text:
What this course is
“Us and them” is one of the oldest structures in politics and one of the hardest to pin down. This seminar asks what happens to a democracy when that line hardens, and what group identity has to do with it.
We start with identity, where the concept comes from and how an attachment to a group becomes a political fact. Then we take the word “polarization” apart, because it names several different things and many arguments in this literature are really arguments about which one is meant. The middle of the term belongs to affective polarization, the tendency to dislike the other side rather than merely to disagree with it, and to the survey items that much of the evidence for it rests on. We end by pushing on the concept: what happens when the dividing line is religion or region rather than party, whether partisan animosity is about identity at all, and how much of the alleged damage to democracy holds up.
The last three sessions belong to your term paper: two of short pitches to the group, and one of optional individual consultation.

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Session 03 goals


read the goals aloud
goal 2 is what the whole session builds to


By the end of today, you will be able to:

Distinguish elite from mass polarization, and ideological divergence from issue alignment.
Explain why two authors can disagree about whether a public is polarized without disagreeing about any fact.
Identify which concept of polarization a given empirical claim depends on.

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Today


0 to 5 min: goals and agenda
say once: core reading was linked wrongly at first, see syllabus
anyone who read the Annual Review has read Fiorina’s side at length



The concept

A word borrowed from physics, and the meanings it picked up

The debate

Is the American public polarized? A 2008 exchange in the Journal of Politics

Abramowitz and Saunders (2008)

“Is polarization a myth?”

Fiorina, Abrams and Pope (2008)

“Misconceptions and misreadings”

What were they disagreeing about?

Pair task and discussion

Wrap-up

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Borrowed from physics


start outside political science
unpolarized light vibrates in every plane, a filter aligns it to one
magnet: charge separated to two poles
what is missing: conflict. Social science added that.
ask: hearing “polarized society”, what do you picture?



In physics, polarization is the orientation of a wave
The original meaning is alignment, orientation, separation
Nothing about conflict or hostility. Social science supplied that.



Figure 1: Two physical meanings of polarization. Light passing a filter ends up aligned in one plane, and a magnet separates charge towards two poles. Neither involves conflict.

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
A family of concepts


grey = before, navy = after
dispersion = spread, bimodality = middle empties
sorting = divides correlate, nobody moves on the x axis
distance = group means
key point: these can move in opposite directions in the same data
flag: this figure returns in the pair task



Broadest usage: alignment, separation, sorting, divergence
At least four mathematically distinct things share the name
They can move in opposite directions in the same data



Figure 2: Four meanings of polarization, grey before and navy after. Dispersion is how spread out opinions are, bimodality is whether the middle empties, sorting is whether two divides become correlated, and distance is how far apart group means are.

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Three further axes


bipolar vs multipolar: US assumes two camps, Europe has seven parties
state vs process: “is polarized” snapshot, “is polarizing” trend
object vs target: who is polarized, and against whom?
pivot: the third axis is where today’s debate starts



Bipolar vs multipolar: nothing requires two camps
State vs process: a snapshot vs a trend
Object vs target: who is polarized against whom?



Figure 3: Bipolar and multipolar configurations. On the left, two camps on one dimension. On the right, several camps spread over several dimensions.

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Elite versus mass


elites: roll-call voting apart since the 1970s, both readings accept it
the fight is over the mass public
ask: what would you need to see in survey data to call a public polarized?
collect two or three answers, keep for the pair task



Elites (legislators, activists): divergence since the 1970s is not disputed (Fiorina et al. 2008)
The mass public: does the electorate follow its elites?
Two further distinctions sit inside that question

Ideological divergence: people move apart on issues, towards the extremes
Issue alignment: positions bundle together, and with party, without anyone moving

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Is the public polarized?


setting: red-blue maps after 2000 and 2004, “culture war” talk
Fiorina, Culture War?: public moderate, only elites polarized
A&S attack it, FAP reply in the same issue
Annual Review: Fiorina’s side at length, optional, not needed today



After 2000 and 2004: red states vs blue states, a “culture war” narrative
Culture War? The Myth of a Polarized America (Fiorina et al. 2006): the public is closely but not deeply divided
Journal of Politics 70 (2), 2008, critique and reply back to back

Abramowitz and Saunders (2008): “Is polarization a myth?”
Fiorina et al. (2008): “Misconceptions and misreadings”

Same data, same decades, opposite verdicts

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Introduction


Converse 1964: ideological thinking confined to a small minority
Fiorina says it still holds, A&S say the world changed
ask: what changed since the 1950s that might make voters more ideological?



Puzzle: Fiorina says today’s voters look like the barely ideological public Converse (2006) described for the 1950s
But much has changed since then

Share with some college education: 19% in 1956, 61% in 2004
Party elites have moved apart for decades

Question: is mass polarization a myth?
They test five of Fiorina’s claims: moderation, partisan and geographic polarization, social cleavages, and voter engagement

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Theory


three claims, one per bullet
the engagement claim is the one that matters for the debate
flag: “whose opinions matter most” is a normative choice of population



Education and elite cues: a more educated public, watching polarized elites, should think more ideologically
The engaged: polarization should be deepest among the interested, informed and active, “whose opinions matter most to candidates and officeholders”
Mobilization: polarization raises the stakes of an election, so it should energize voters, not turn them off

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Research design


coding choices: collapse to lib, mod, con, don’t knows to the middle, then an index
FAP attack exactly this, ask them to remember it



Data: American National Election Studies 1972 to 2004, 2004 National Exit Poll
Ideological consistency: seven issues, each collapsed to liberal, moderate or conservative

Score = |number of liberal positions minus number of conservative positions|
A 16-item scale for 2004, recoded to 11 points

Engagement: interest, knowledge and participation, split into thirds
Partisan polarization: correlation of party identification with ideology over time
Geography and religion: red vs blue state voters, logit of the Bush vote on religiosity

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Results: consistency


top row: 24, 29, 33
gap: nonvoters flat 18 to 19, college grads 36 to 49
inter-item correlation .20, .26, .32
name the concept: constraint








Figure 4: Share of respondents holding consistently liberal or consistently conservative positions across seven issue questions, by decade and by group. It rises for every engaged group and stays flat for nonvoters. Source: Abramowitz and Saunders (2008), Table 1.




The average correlation between the seven items rises from .20 to .26 to .32

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Results: the engaged


same mean 6.1 vs 6.2, SD 1.5 vs 2.8
ask: is the right panel bimodal? mass both sides, dip at the middle
consistent lib/con: 13 and 19 left, 32 and 39 right










Figure 5: The least engaged third of 2004 NES respondents on an 11-point liberal-conservative policy scale, clustered on the moderate positions. Mean 6.1, SD 1.5. Source: Abramowitz and Saunders (2008), Figure 1, panel A.










Figure 6: The most engaged third on the same scale, spread towards both ends with a dip at the middle. Mean 6.2, SD 2.8. Source: Abramowitz and Saunders (2008), Figure 1, panel B.





Same mean, nearly double the spread. The engaged third is 37% of respondents and close to half of all voters.

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Results: sorting


r = .32 in 1972, .44 in 1992, .63 in 2004
among the engaged .47 to .77
ask: dispersion, bimodality, sorting or distance? answer: sorting








Figure 7: Correlation of party identification with liberal-conservative identification in the NES, 1972 to 2004. It rises from .32 to .63, most steeply after 1992. Source: Abramowitz and Saunders (2008), Figure 3.




Among the engaged the same correlation runs from .47 to .77, and the gap between the parties’ mean ideology doubles

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Results: geography


middle rows: battlegrounds 24, 24, 15, 12
uncompetitive states 18 to 31
national margin tiny, average state margin nearly doubles
flag: FAP say election returns cannot measure polarization at all








Figure 8: Competitiveness of four closely contested presidential elections. The national margin stays small, while the average state margin nearly doubles and the number of battleground states halves. Source: Abramowitz and Saunders (2008), Table 5.

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Results: other evidence


quick, one number each
also results FAP rule out as evidence, hold that thought



Religion: among white voters, religiosity predicts the Bush vote better than any other social characteristic

P(Bush vote) .34 for the least religious, .81 for the most religious

Engagement in 2004: turnout 54% to 61%, persuasion attempts 32% to 48%

Voters feeling strongly about Bush, either way, were the most likely to vote and campaign

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Conclusion


read the Pogo line
it sums up their reading of the whole debate



Polarization is not just an elite phenomenon
The centre is held by the least interested, informed and active
Elite divisions “reflect real divisions within the American electorate”
Polarization energizes the electorate rather than turning it off


“We have met the enemy and he is us” (Abramowitz and Saunders 2008, quoting Pogo)

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Introduction


first move: rule out a class of evidence before replying
ask: do you accept that a vote cannot show polarization?
keep it short, the pair task returns to it



A point-by-point reply to the five criticisms
Before the reply, a rule about evidence:

Votes, election returns and approval ratings “can not be used as evidence of polarization, for or against”

Everything else follows from that rule and from one definition

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Theory


board sketch: same voters, candidates differ first on economics, then on morals
the vote divides along whichever dimension the candidates chose
the voters did not change, the candidates did



Polarization = movement from the centre towards the extremes, so the test is rising bimodality
Sorting is something else: party groups grow more distinct while the overall distribution stays put
Centrist voters register polarized choices when the candidates polarize, without moving themselves
So a changed relationship in the data may sit on the candidates’ side, not the voters’

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Research design


contrast: FAP raw distributions, A&S recoded indices
name it: a measurement disagreement, not a definitional one



Raw distributions instead of recoded and aggregated indices
Ideological self-placement in three surveys: NES, GSS and Gallup, 1970s to 2000s
The same NES issue scales as A&S, compared position by position, 1984 vs 2004
Pew Research Center: party differences on 40 items, 1987 to 2007
Abortion positions of strong partisans in 2004

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Results: raw data


jobs and standard of living: centre down 2, left up 3, right up 4
the only issue with any polarization
the rest shift as a whole, or not at all
brackets: don’t knows as moderates, A&S’s coding choice








Figure 9: Percentage point change in each position of six NES issue scales between 1984 and 2004, from extremely liberal (left) to extremely conservative (right). Numbers in brackets treat “don’t knows” as moderates. Source: Fiorina et al. (2008), Table 1.




Only jobs and standard of living loses its centre to both extremes

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Results: limited sorting


Pew line: 10 to 14 points over 20 years
sorting granted, but far less than among elites
ask: does a 4 point move over 20 years look like polarization?








Figure 10: Average percentage point difference between Republican and Democratic identifiers on 40 political and social questions, 1987 to 2007. It grows from 10 to 14 points. Source: Fiorina et al. (2008), Figure 1, from Pew Research Center data.




Party sorting “certainly has occurred”, but far less than among elites

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Results: the rest


abortion: the textbook sorting case, still a third and two fifths out of step
one NES issue splits red and blue majorities: homosexual adoption
mobilization, not polarization, for 2004: a factual disagreement
religion vs class: they deny ever making the claim



Abortion, 2004: a third of strong Democrats and two fifths of strong Republicans break with their party’s position
Red vs blue states: majorities disagree on one NES issue, homosexual adoption
2004 turnout: the parties’ ground game rather than polarization, with party contacts up 8 points
Religion vs class: A&S attribute a claim to them that they say they never made

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Conclusion


one line: sorting yes, polarization no
ask: after both papers, what do they agree on? put it on the board
you need that list for the pair task



Without “multiple recodings and aggregations”, the A&S case “disappears”
Sorting yes, polarization no
Red-blue divides are a “misleading exaggeration”
2004 engagement rests on one election and ignores mobilization
“No reason to revise the conclusions of Culture War?”

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Two definitions


read both quotations out
FAP: shape of one distribution. A&S: subgroups inside it.
neither is wrong about the data
put the question to the room before the pair task



“adopting the common sense notion of polarization as a movement from the center toward the extremes, one searches in vain for evidence of increasing bimodality” (Fiorina et al. 2008)



“the existence of polarization in a society does not just depend on the overall distribution of political attitudes among the public. It also depends on whether there are differences between the views of important subgroups” (Abramowitz and Saunders 2008)




One asks about the shape of a distribution, the other about differences between groups inside it

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Pair task


10 min, in pairs
put the four-panel figure back up if asked
walk around, push “both are right” pairs to say about what


For each claim, note what evidence each side uses and which concept from Figure 2 or the three axes it rests on.

“The public is more polarized than in the 1980s.”
“Democrats and Republicans are further apart.”
“The public is polarized where it counts.”
“Voters are divided: look at the red and blue map.”
“The data show it.”

Then decide: is the disagreement about a definition, a measurement or a fact?

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
The mapping


reveal only after the pairs report
row by row: pairs first, table second






Table 1: Five disputed claims in the 2008 exchange, the evidence each side uses for them, and the concept or measurement choice the disagreement turns on.











Claim
A&S look at
FAP look at
What is at stake




The public is polarized
Consistency across issues, 24 to 33%
Each item’s raw distribution, the middle holds
Constraint vs bimodality


The parties are further apart
Party ID and ideology, r .32 to .63
The same fact, called sorting
Sorting vs polarization


Polarized where it counts
The engaged third, SD 2.8
The public as a whole
Which population


Voters are divided
Votes, approval, red vs blue states
Not evidence, it reflects the candidates
Choices vs positions


The data show it
Recoded items, don’t knows as moderates, an index
Raw position-by-position change
Measurement

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Three kinds of dispute


this answers goal 2
stress: they agree on most facts
elites diverged, sorting happened, self-placement barely moved
what is left: mostly naming, some coding, a little fact



Mostly definitional: both accept that party sorting happened. They disagree about whether to call it polarization.
Partly measurement: coding “don’t knows” as moderates and aggregating items into an index change the answer
A little substantive: was 2004 turnout driven by polarization or by party mobilization? Does religion outweigh class?








Important


“Is the public polarized?” has no answer until you say what you mean with “polarization”. Two authors can read the same data and reach opposite verdicts, because they are measuring different concepts.

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Questions for the group


plenary to 80 min
pick two, not all four
the last one bridges to next week



If both sides accept that sorting happened, what exactly is left to disagree about?
Is a public polarized if its engaged third is? Whose opinions should count?
If votes cannot show polarization, what evidence could?
Does any of this travel to a multiparty system like Germany’s?

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Recap: takeaways


ask for one takeaway before revealing the list



Polarization is a family of concepts: dispersion, bimodality, sorting, distance, plus three axes
Elites diverged without dispute. The contested question is the mass public.
A&S find rising consistency and sorting, deepest among the engaged
FAP find a stable middle and call the rest sorting
Most of the dispute is about which concept and which population, some about coding, little about facts

title: Session 03: What is political polarization?
text:
Recap: learning goals


goal by goal
ask for each answer before revealing it


Goal 1. Elite vs mass, divergence vs alignment

Elite polarization concerns office holders and activists, mass polarization the electorate
Divergence means moving towards the extremes. Alignment means positions bundling together, and with party.

Goal 2. Disagreeing without disagreeing about a fact

A&S and FAP largely agree on the facts, but attach the word to different concepts and populations

Goal 3. Which concept a claim depends on

Ask what distribution changed, in whom, and whether it is positions or choices

1 min
sell the move: from what people think to how they feel

From where people stand to how they feel about the other side

text:
Before you go


say it out loud even if the session overran
they cannot find this out late
point at the syllabus, no format questions here



The term paper is empirical: it confronts a claim with data you analyse yourself
It is two things: the written paper, and the code that reproduces its analysis
Any technology, R, Python, Stata or anything else. Nothing is prescribed.
What is required is that a result comes out of a script that runs again, not out of clicks nobody can retrace
The detail is in the syllabus







Note


Two voluntary platforms, neither needed to pass. DataCamp gives you six months of premium access through the course group, for self-paced practice in R and data analysis. Duolingo Math is there if you want to warm up the maths.
